prompt: Which of these is an asset at Vereda that is not data?

choices.text: The records database's backups, kept off site
choices.why: Backups are data.

choices.text: The portal being up
choices.why: Right: a clinic without its agenda cannot work.

choices.text: The exam PDFs patients upload each week
choices.why: Those are data.

choices.text: The patients' phone numbers used for reminders
choices.why: Contact data.

prompt: For which property does payment status matter most?

choices.text: Confidentiality, since payments are private
choices.why: Low here: knowing a session is paid harms nobody.

choices.text: Availability, since the gateway goes down
choices.why: Medium; integrity is the high one.

choices.text: None of the three
choices.why: Integrity is high.

choices.text: Integrity
choices.why: Right: nobody steals it, somebody changes it. That is T01.

prompt: Why does the lesson say integrity of clinical notes matters as much as their confidentiality?

choices.text: A changed note leads to the wrong treatment
choices.why: Right: a clinical risk, the objective PASTA found missing.

choices.text: The LGPD only protects integrity
choices.why: The law covers both, and that is not the argument.

choices.text: Notes are encrypted, so they cannot leak
choices.why: Nothing says they are, and leaks remain possible.

choices.text: Physiotherapists rarely read old notes
choices.why: They read them before each session.

prompt: Match each asset to the threat the lesson's table lists against it.
An asset on the list has no threat beside it. What does the lesson read into that?

choices.text: That the asset is safe and can leave the list
choices.why: Absence of a threat is not evidence of safety.

choices.text: That the asset is worthless
choices.why: Value and threats are separate questions.

choices.text: A question: well protected, or nobody looked
choices.why: Right. The spreadsheet of clinics was the second kind.

choices.text: That the DFD is wrong
choices.why: Possibly, but the lesson asks first.

prompt: What two things decide what an actor can do, in this lesson?

choices.text: Motive and nationality, as a profile would put them
choices.why: Nationality decides nothing here.

choices.text: Skill and the tools they own, as a pentest would rate
choices.why: Skill is part of capability; access is missing.

choices.text: Starting access and capability
choices.why: Right: the two axes of the figure.

choices.text: Their name and their job title
choices.why: Actors are roles, not characters.

prompt: What stops the curious receptionist, according to the actors table?

choices.text: Narrower roles, and an access log somebody reads
choices.why: Right: the receptionist already has access, so the controls are inside.

choices.text: A firewall between the clinic network and the cloud account
choices.why: The receptionist is inside it.

choices.text: A second factor at sign-in
choices.why: The receptionist signs in legitimately.

choices.text: Rate limits on sign-in
choices.why: Nobody is guessing passwords.

prompt: Why did "someone close to a patient" change how the team saw T08, the reminder SMS?

choices.text: That actor works at the SMS provider
choices.why: That is a different actor.

choices.text: That actor breaks the SMS encryption on the way to the phone
choices.why: No breaking is needed.

choices.text: That actor sends the reminders
choices.why: The worker sends them.

choices.text: They hold the phone and want where and when
choices.why: Right: the most to gain and the least skill needed.

prompt: Which of these actors start with some access already? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the former employee
choices.why: An account nobody switched off.

choices.text: someone close to a patient
choices.why: The patient's phone or password.

choices.text: the extortion group
choices.why: Nothing but time.

choices.text: the SMS provider employee
choices.why: Every message Vereda sends.

prompt: What is the test of whether an actor deserves its place on the list?

choices.text: It has a detailed persona with a backstory
choices.why: That is fiction, not a role.

choices.text: It changes a decision
choices.why: Right: it makes somebody ask a new question about the design.

choices.text: It appears in a threat intelligence report
choices.why: Several useful actors do not.

choices.text: It is skilled
choices.why: Most harm needs no skill.

prompt: What is an abuse case?

choices.text: A feature seen by somebody who wants what it was not meant to give
choices.why: Right. Same feature, different intent.

choices.text: A bug report
choices.why: It is written before any code.

choices.text: A pentest finding
choices.why: It describes intent, not a result.

choices.text: A list of attack tools
choices.why: It names no technique.

prompt: Why is a mitigation drawn as a use case in the misuse diagram?

choices.text: Because UML requires it
choices.why: It is the method's choice, for a reason.

choices.text: So it gets an owner and a place in the backlog
choices.why: Right, rather than a note nobody schedules.

choices.text: To make the diagram symmetric and easier to read on a slide
choices.why: The reason is ownership.

choices.text: Because mitigations are external entities
choices.why: They are features of the system.

prompt: Put the four parts of an abuse case in order.
items: what they do, in the feature's terms
what the system should do instead

prompt: What makes an abuse case more than a threat?

choices.text: It names the attacker
choices.why: A threat names an actor too.

choices.text: It has a CWE number
choices.why: That is lesson 4's stage 5.

choices.text: It says what right looks like
choices.why: Right: half a requirement already.

choices.text: It is longer and more detailed than the threat
choices.why: Length adds nothing; the fourth line does.

prompt: In a misuse case diagram, a misuse case ___ a use case, and a mitigating use case mitigates it.
How many new threats did the abuse cases add to the list?
Which abuse case does the lesson call the most serious of the new ones?

choices.text: A7, the former employee's account
choices.why: Serious, but A9 hands over the account.

choices.text: A8, reading the agenda week by week
choices.why: A9 is called the most serious.

choices.text: A10, the forged webhook
choices.why: That one is not new: it is T01.

choices.text: A9, changing the phone number
choices.why: Right: it redirects reminders and password resets.

prompt: Match each threat to its STRIDE letter.

pairs.left: T16, another session reads the agenda
T05, a note changed with no record

prompt: A10 repeats T01. Why does the lesson keep it?

choices.text: To make the count reach ten
choices.why: Counts are not the point.

choices.text: It describes the flaw in the words of the feature it breaks
choices.why: Right: that is what a product owner needs to see.

choices.text: Because T01 was closed
choices.why: It is not closed yet.

choices.text: It is a different threat
choices.why: It is the same flaw.

prompt: Why does the first scenario say the refusal is the same as for an exam that does not exist?

choices.text: It is easier to code
choices.why: Ease is not the reason.

choices.text: Because the exam is deleted once somebody else asks for it
choices.why: It exists; the answer hides that.

choices.text: Because the law requires a 404 for any refused request
choices.why: No law is cited.

choices.text: A forbidden answer tells the asker the exam exists
choices.why: Right: an output, in lesson 6's sense.

prompt: Which habits does the lesson give for abuse-case tests? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: test the refusal, not only the success
choices.why: A suite of successes passes on a portal that shows everything.

choices.text: make the refusal indistinguishable
choices.why: So it leaks nothing.

choices.text: record the attempt
choices.why: So somebody can notice it.

choices.text: name the attack technique in the scenario
choices.why: The scenarios deliberately do not.

prompt: After the abuse cases, how many spoofing threats does threats.csv hold?
Why do the scenarios avoid words like IDOR or account takeover?

choices.text: Behaviour tests catch the flaw by any route
choices.why: Right, and the product owner can read it.

choices.text: Those words are not allowed in test names
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: Attackers could read the tests in the repository and learn from them
choices.why: That is not the argument.

choices.text: They are too new to be understood
choices.why: Age is not the reason.

prompt: Vereda lets patients add a family member who can book for them. Crossing that use case with someone close to a patient, which abuse case comes first?

choices.text: The family member forges the payment webhook
choices.why: Unrelated to this use case.

choices.text: The family member uploads a large PDF
choices.why: That is T10, not this actor's motive.

choices.text: They keep watching after the patient objects
choices.why: Right: so the patient must see and remove who has access.

choices.text: The family member phishes a receptionist to reach the console
choices.why: Possible, and not the first case this use case raises.

prompt: For the same feature, which line completes the abuse case?

choices.text: The family member is warned not to misuse it
choices.why: A warning is not a control.

choices.text: Reception decides case by case
choices.why: That puts the burden on people, not the design.

choices.text: The patient sees who has access and removes it in one step
choices.why: Right: what the system should do instead.

choices.text: The feature is logged for the auditor
choices.why: A log alone does not stop the watching.

prompt: An abuse case crosses a use case with an ___ from the actors list.
